title: When Ferns Took Over the World and Set It on Fire
summary:
Picture a world covered in ferns — not just a few, but everywhere, like a giant green carpet. That's what parts of Europe looked like 201 million years ago, after massive volcanic eruptions caused a mass extinction. The volcanoes pumped out so much carbon dioxide that the planet heated up by 5 to 10 degrees Celsius. Forests collapsed, and fast-growing ferns took over.

But there was a scary side effect: the ferns kept catching fire. Scientists from Utrecht University figured this out by studying ancient pollen and spores from deep underground. They used a simple, low-cost method: they measured how dark the tiny fossils were. Normally, fossils get darker the deeper they're buried because of heat and pressure. But here, the darkest fossils were from the time of the fern takeover, not from the deepest layers.

That darkness came from wildfire smoke. The team also found lots of charcoal and special chemicals from smoke in the same layers. It all pointed to a world on fire. The ferns created savannah-like landscapes that dried out easily and burned often. These wildfires might have even helped the ferns by clearing out other plants.

This research helps us understand how life on Earth responds to extreme climate change. Today, as our planet warms, we might see more wildfires too. Learning from the past could help us prepare for the future.
why_it_matters: Even though these fires happened millions of years ago, they teach us that changes in plants and weather can make wildfires more common—something we see today when forests dry out.

background_read: This happened during a period called the Triassic, long before dinosaurs like T. rex walked the Earth; after the extinction, dinosaurs eventually became the new rulers.
Utrecht University (in the Netherlands) is known for studying ancient climates using tiny fossils, just like detectives.
Today, scientists worry that modern climate change could also lead to more wildfires, so studying ancient fires helps us prepare.
Article_Structure: WHAT: They discovered that after a mass extinction 201 million years ago, ferns took over and caused many wildfires by studying dark-colored fossil spores and finding charcoal.
WHERE: In ancient rock layers under Europe, with the study led from the Netherlands.
WHY: To learn how life responds to extreme climate change and help us deal with wildfires today.

perspectives.description: They are glad to have evidence that extreme warming in the past led to more fires, which supports their warnings about our future.
They might worry that if ancient ferns caused fires, today's climate change could mean more danger near their homes.
They see that even after disasters, nature finds a way to recover, though it might look very different.
